U.S. forces have helped Persian Gulf producers move more than 1.5 billion barrels out of the Strait of Hormuz since the Iran war began, Adm. Brad Cooper, the commander of U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM), said during a visit to the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday.
More than 3,000 commercial vessels have successfully transited the Strait of Hormuz with support from CENTCOM forces over the last six months, the U.S. military said.
"We continue to stand shoulder to shoulder with our Gulf partners and the shipping industry," said Cooper.
"This visit underscores our strong commitment to continued freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz."
American forces have successfully cleared the Strait of Hormuz's international shipping lanes of sea mines laid by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), according to the U.S. Central Command.
The U.S. military said that the 95% success rate of ships navigating the Strait of Hormuz without incident in recent months is "clearly demonstrating that the United States and regional partners control the international waterway."
Oil flows out of the Strait of Hormuz, and the whole Middle East has recovered in the past two months, according to various tanker-tracking services. Some estimates put the flows at the Strait of Hormuz at already exceeding pre-war levels, excluding Iranian exports.
However, threats to shipping in the area have not subsided . On the contrary, the escalating Saudi-Houthi tensions could disrupt the recovering flows, while Iran has claimed dozens of hits on tankers in the Persian Gulf and in the Strait of Hormuz.
At any rate, the market continues to price in a prolonged disruption and continued inefficient oil shipments, which have hiked shipping costs to record highs, further raising the cost of crude oil for buyers and ultimately, for the end consumers.
Oil prices fell in Asian trade on Monday, but Brent Crude remained above $115 per barrel, and WTI was still above the $100 mark, as hostilities between Yemen's Houthis and Saudi Arabia, as well as Iranian attacks on tankers in the Persian Gulf, continue.

items.title: As Trump brags about U.S. oil and gas company profits, his stocks gained millions during Iran war - CBS News
items.summary: As Trump brags about U.S. oil and gas company profits, his stocks gained millions during Iran war  CBS News
items.content:
Washington — As President Trump boasts about how much money the U.S. oil and gas industry is making from the war with Iran, the president's personal holdings in oil and gas are now worth between $22.5 million and $81.6 million, compared with $12.6 million to $46 million at the end of 2025, according to a new report by Democrats on the Congressional Joint Economic Committee.
The stocks the president holds have increased in value by an average of 43% since the end of 2025, the Democratic minority said, based on data from LSEG Data Analytics. The report also found the president purchased between $4.7 million and $17.5 million in oil and gas stocks between March, after the war began, and the end of August, which is the most recently available data. He also sold between $2 million and $5.4 million in oil and gas stocks in the same timeframe, the minority found.
The report was obtained exclusively by CBS News and is based on the president's financial filings with the Office of Government Ethics. Filers are only required to report transaction ranges, not specific amounts.
But as Americans are paying significantly higher gas prices due to downstream effects from the war, Mr. Trump on Saturday night in Georgia bragged that U.S. oil and gas companies are "making hundreds of billions of dollars."
"And while oil prices are temporarily high and will be falling dramatically in a short period of time, as soon as that war's over, because there's so much oil," he told the crowd. "All in the Hormuz Strait, there are ships waiting to come, we're getting them out so fast. The United States oil and gas business is making hundreds of billions of dollars. … Our country is making hundreds of billions of dollars because of what's happened in the Middle East."
The president added that his advisers told him not to mention how much money the oil and gas industry is making from the chaos in the Middle East.
The wealthiest person to serve as president, Mr. Trump has a vast stock portfolio with holdings in all sectors of the economy. He has executed thousands of stock and securities trades this year, worth hundreds of millions of dollars, CBS News has previously reported . The White House says Mr. Trump doesn't make trading decisions himself, and his money managers try to replicate major stock indices.
"President Trump only acts in the best interests of the American public – which is why they overwhelmingly reelected him to this office, despite years of lies and false accusations against him and his businesses," said White House spokesman Davis Ingle.
Ingle said Mr. Trump's stock and bond portfolio is "independently managed by third-party financial institutions" and all his holdings are "maintained in discretionary accounts and invested through computer-based model portfolios that automatically replicate recognized indexes."
"Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold," Ingle added. "All investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers. There are no conflicts of interest."
In a July 2026 interview with CNBC , Mr. Trump said his son, Eric Trump, also handles his finances.
Energy stocks have surged as the Iran war pushed oil and gasoline prices to their highest levels in years, driving profits for oil companies . The share prices of energy companies that are listed on the S&P 500 jumped more than 50% since the start of the year, easily outpacing the broader S&P 500's roughly 11% jump.
In early February, before the Iran war began at the end of February , nationwide, the average cost of a gallon of regular gas was $2.87, and a gallon of diesel cost $3.68. Now, eight months later , it's $4.29, with diesel at $6.28 per gallon. The global benchmark for crude oil, Brent, is also hovering above $115 a barrel, compared to less than $75 the day before the war began.
"Trump's Iran War has forced Americans to pay much more at the pump while Big Oil rakes in profits and the president's own stock wealth in the oil and gas industry continues to balloon," said Sen. Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the Joint Economic Committee. "As Trump — the country's highest ranking public employee — continues to own and trade stocks in companies that stand to benefit from his decisions, his actions raise major concerns about conflicts of interest."
Presidents, vice presidents and members of Congress are allowed to own, buy and sell stocks while in office, although insider trading laws still apply.
The minority said the president's stock purchases or total value may be even higher, since he has not yet reported transactions for September or October.
Among the nine stocks that make up the largest oil and gas holdings in Mr. Trump's portfolio, Chevron and ExxonMobil represent the most significant portion. He owns up to $23.1 million in Chevron stock and up to $18.4 million in ExxonMobil, which saw their stock prices grow nearly 25% and nearly 22% in value, respectively, since Feb. 20.
Democrats on the committee estimated American families have spent an average of $856 more on gas since the war began.
There are occasional reminders that pronouncements the president makes affect policies. In August, Mr. Trump called out ExxonMobil and Chevron by name for making "too much money" on fuel profits.
"They're making too much money, okay?" he said in the Oval Office. "Based on a shortage, they're making too much money. I don't like it. And I should be the last one to say because I'm a big free enterprise guy, nobody bigger."
Energy stock purchases and sales make up a small portion of the president's overall net worth, which Forbes estimated to be roughly $7 billion as of September.
In August, CBS News reviewed the president's oil and gas trades. One notable large transaction was on April 7, the day the president declared a ceasefire in the war. His investment accounts sold between $500,000 and $1 million of ExxonMobil stock, according to a financial disclosure report Mr. Trump filed in late June. The company's share price closed at $163.91 on April 7, before Mr. Trump announced the ceasefire that evening, and it opened down over 6% at $153.52 on April 8.
The cost of living continues to be a top issue for voters.
Last week, Mr. Trump accused Iran of trying to drive up oil prices ahead of next week's U.S. elections.
"Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of Oil prior to the U.S. Midterm Election," he wrote on Truth Social. "They are even making up fake hits, mines, and everything else, because more Oil is coming through the Hormuz Strait now than it did even prior to the beginning of the Conflict."
Since Mr. Trump launched the war with Iran on Feb. 28, the conflict has stymied oil exports in the region, particularly in the Strait of Hormuz. Oil shipments from the Middle East have climbed since then as exporters look for alternate routes and some traffic in the strait is restored. But the disruptions, constricted supply and uncertainty have pushed up prices, even in the U.S., which is the world's largest exporter of total oil products.
The president has made some efforts to bring down fuel prices, including by making a deal with Russia to purchase Russian diesel fuel and waiving sanctions he had just signed into law. But that fuel from Russia, a controversial move, is a drop in the bucket of the United States' massive demand, and does little to lower diesel prices.
On Thursday, the president announced he would invoke the Defense Production Act to spend $150 million to boost gasoline and diesel production.
Mr. Trump has said gas prices will "drop through the floor" once the war is over, but even if that's the case, it's not clear when the war will end.
The president has not ruled out restarting strikes on Iran after the midterms. U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz told the Financial Times the war could last another year, although he said he hopes the Iranian leaders "come to the table" before that.
This story published first on CBS News at 9:30 a.m. on Oct. 26, 2026.

items.content:
US Stock Futures Point Higher as Crude Oil Retreats and Investors Await Fed Meeting: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq, Wall Street
Dow Jones on phone ©Adobe Stock Images US stock futures indicated a higher opening on Monday as investors assessed a decline in crude oil prices following two sessions of losses on Wall Street, with attention turning to the Federal Reserve's monetary policy announcement and earnings from major technology companies.
The expected advance follows a decline in the Nasdaq Composite to its lowest closing level since early August on Friday, while the S&P 500 finished at a one-month low.
Lower share prices following the recent sell-off may also encourage some investors to increase their equity holdings.
However, uncertainty surrounding artificial intelligence investment, monetary policy and developments in the Middle East remains a consideration for financial markets.
Crude Oil Futures Decline After US Military Reports Export Recovery
US crude oil futures fell more than 2% on Monday, reversing part of the previous week's increase.
The decline followed an announcement by US Central Command (CENTCOM) concerning its support for oil exports from the Gulf region.
According to CENTCOM, US forces have assisted regional partners in exporting more than 1.5 billion barrels of crude oil since the summer.
The military command also said more than 3,000 commercial vessels had successfully travelled through the Strait of Hormuz with US support over the past six months.
The figures indicated that maritime transport and crude shipments had continued despite disruptions associated with the conflict involving Iran.
Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, said the recovery in exports was helping to reduce concerns about the potential impact of further military action.
"The ongoing recovery in Middle Eastern exports is easing some of the concerns surrounding the possibility of renewed American and Israeli attacks on Iran," Mould said.
Oil prices had risen during the previous week as attacks by Iran-aligned Houthi forces in Yemen against Saudi Arabia added to concerns about regional supply disruptions.
Reports that the United States and Israel could resume military operations against Iran after the November midterm elections also contributed to the increase.
On Friday, US crude futures climbed nearly 4%, returning to levels above $100 per barrel, while Brent crude reached a six-month high.
The subsequent decline on Monday reduced some of the pressure associated with elevated energy prices.
Federal Reserve Expected to Maintain Interest Rates
The Federal Reserve's monetary policy announcement on Wednesday will be among the principal events for US financial markets this week.
The central bank is widely expected to leave its benchmark interest rate unchanged.
Investors will examine the accompanying statement for indications of how policymakers are evaluating inflation and the possibility of additional rate increases.
Market expectations continue to favour a quarter-percentage-point increase at the Fed's December meeting.
The outlook for interest rates is particularly relevant to equity valuations and financing costs, including those associated with investment in technology infrastructure.
Trading volumes could remain relatively limited before the announcement as market participants await further guidance.
Technology Earnings Could Influence AI Investment Expectations
Corporate earnings will provide another source of information for investors, particularly following recent declines in technology shares.
Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN), Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) and Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL), Google's parent company, are scheduled to report quarterly financial results.
Their announcements will be monitored for evidence of demand trends, profitability and spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Investors have been assessing whether revenue generated from AI products and services will support the substantial capital expenditure required to develop computing capacity.
Concerns about financing requirements and potential investment returns contributed to the recent weakness in technology stocks.
The upcoming results could provide further information about spending plans, operating costs and management expectations for future growth.
Given the companies' substantial influence on major US equity indices, their financial performance could also affect broader market movements.
US equities declined on Friday following a sell-off during Thursday's session, with all three major indices finishing lower.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average recorded the largest percentage decline, falling 652.82 points, or 1.2%, to close at 52,215.16. The index retreated from a one-month closing high reached in the preceding session.
The S&P 500 declined 39.75 points, or 0.5%, to 7,623.68, its lowest closing level in approximately one month.
The Nasdaq Composite fell 53.52 points, or 0.2%, to 25,955.34, ending the session at its lowest level since early August.
For the week, the Dow Jones advanced 0.4%, despite Friday's decline.
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq recorded weekly losses of 0.5% and 0.7%, respectively.
The market movements reflected concerns about AI-related investments, higher oil prices and uncertainty ahead of the Federal Reserve's next decision.
Oil Price Increase Affects Airline and Energy Shares
Friday's sector performance showed differences between companies exposed to higher energy costs and those operating in the oil industry.
Airline shares declined as crude prices increased, with the NYSE Arca Airline Index falling 2.6%.
Fuel is a significant operating expense for airlines, making higher oil prices relevant to their cost outlook.
Gold mining companies also recorded losses after the price of gold declined.
The NYSE Arca Gold Bugs Index fell 2.2%, while pharmaceutical and retail stocks also experienced selling pressure.
Oil services shares moved in the opposite direction.
The Philadelphia Oil Service Index gained 5.5% as crude prices advanced, reflecting increases among companies providing equipment and services to oil producers.
The different sector performances illustrated the effects of commodity price movements on companies with varying operating costs and revenue exposures.
Investors Assess Monetary Policy and Geopolitical Risks
Monday's expected gains suggest that US equities could recover part of their recent losses, with lower oil prices providing a change from the conditions that affected markets late last week.
The Federal Reserve's decision on Wednesday and earnings from major technology companies will provide further information for investors assessing interest rates, corporate profitability and AI-related capital expenditure.
Developments in the Middle East will also remain relevant because of their potential implications for oil shipments, energy prices and inflation.
Market movements during the week will reflect how investors respond to these economic, corporate and geopolitical developments.

items.title: Cadence reveals Maestro, fine-tuned AI models built to run specialized chip design agents, with early access coming for 'select customers' in Q4 2026 - Tom's Hardware
items.summary: <a href="https://news.google.
items.content:
Cadence, one of the largest electronic design automation (EDA) companies, has unveiled Maestro, its new portfolio of domain-specialized AI models tailored for its chip design agents, in a press release sent just ahead of earnings. In initial results compared with general-purpose AI models, Cadence claims up to a 30% improvement in the quality of results and that Maestro effectively uses fewer tokens for the same task, with up to 5x the token efficiency. The first models "are available to select early access customers" in Q4 2026, and customers may run them on Cadence's cloud, public clouds, or customer-controlled on-premises environments and post-train them on their own "proprietary data, designs, and workflows." To learn more about Maestro, we spoke with two Cadence executives: Rob Knoth, senior group director of strategy and new ventures, and Paul Cunningham, senior vice president and general manager.
This approach is distinct from Synopsys' own specialized model, GPT-Synopsys , which will run on OpenAI-hosted infrastructure, without using customer data to train the model. The models of both EDA giants, announced less than a month apart, now split on where a customer's design data goes. Where they might not differ is why: Paul Cunningham, senior vice president and general manager at Cadence, told Tom's Hardware Premium that agent costs have "really started to explode," adding, "And I think the world realized so." That makes it a natural step, he said, to move more of the agents' iterating "into the weights of the models themselves."
(Image credit: Cadence) Maestro takes this step through Cadence's AI Super Agents , which "interpret design intent, decompose tasks" and "orchestrate the Maestro portfolio with other leading frontier and open-weight models," evaluating trade-offs to guide decisions with domain expertise. It also uses reinforcement learning (RL), where Cadence's "deterministic solvers evaluate outputs against engineering objectives, constraints and ground truth," and, importantly, the results feed back into the models for improvement.
The models include Nvidia's Nemotron , and customers can run the customer-data training step themselves with Cadence's fine-tuning harness, potentially "on their own GPUs, on their own network," Cunningham said. He added that Nemotron, specifically, was "giving really solid results and actually improving very, very fast."
One constant that keeps popping up with agentic EDA is the need to nail down what the numbers actually measure. In chip design, quality of results usually refers to the design's power, performance, and area, though Cadence didn't specify what its 30% figure measures. Both it and the 5x token efficiency figure are measured against "a general-purpose foundation model," which Cadence told us is the open-source model Maestro started from before its training. The company wouldn't name the foundational AI model that Maestro is derived from beyond mentioning that it is "one of the leading open source models that's very competitive with commercial frontier models."
Cadence credits the token savings to balancing its EDA and system design automation (SDA) "tool calls with LLM invocations." As an analogy, Cunningham said, "You don't need to drive to Safeway in the jet engine," and you want to use "the right model at the right time for the right task."
Runtime does matter, too: as Rob Knoth, senior group director of strategy and new ventures at Cadence, told Tom's Hardware Premium in September that a tool call could take anywhere from hours to days to return a value, while the AI industry's training loops are "used to minutes." Efficiency could also lower costs, since Maestro use counts toward Cadence's agent pricing, a subscription with a consumption allowance and charges for use beyond it, Cunningham said. He didn't say whether the token savings cut a customer's bill.
Being flexible for the customer is a key element of any solution, and for Cadence's competitor Synopsys, this lies in Autopilot , which Synopsys says allows customers to "choose among commercial, open-source, and fine-tuned language models" across "Synopsys-managed and customer-managed deployments," with cloud or on-premises infrastructure. For agent security , such as sandboxing, Cadence says it's working with Nvidia on an integration with Nvidia's OpenShell Reference Architecture, which Nvidia launched last week, naming both Cadence and Synopsys. These options can help protect customer intellectual property.
A portfolio of domain-specialized AI models for Cadence's AI Super Agents
A specialized model that operates Synopsys' tools directly
Post-trained LLMs, trained decision models and agent skills, blended with frontier and open-weight models, including Nemotron
Cadence's cloud, public clouds or customer-controlled on-premises environments
Customers can post-train it on their own data, designs and workflows, with Cadence's fine-tuning tools
Up to 30% higher quality of results and up to 5x token efficiency vs. a general-purpose foundation model, the unnamed open-source model Maestro started from (initial results; measure not stated)
First models to select early-access customers in Q4 2026
Socionext, Silicon Labs (Nvidia as partner), frontier AI labs
Subscription with a usage allowance, then charged by use
Not disclosed; Synopsys and OpenAI share revenue under their deal
Cadence has had a busy 12 months with customers and agents alike. During Cadence's July earnings call, CEO Anirudh Devgan said ChipStack, its design and verification agent, "has more than 20 customer engagements," and ViraStack, its custom and analog agent, "more than 25 customer engagements." Socionext said just last week that it was applying InnoStack. Silicon Labs has also credited ChipStack with accelerating debugging, and both companies say they are watching Maestro next.
Cadence's agentic consolidation began with its acquisition of ChipStack back in November 2025. In June 2026, the company claimed that its agent had reached Level 5 autonomy, which we explored in detail . In September, Knoth teased Maestro's ingredients to Tom's Hardware Premium a month early, two days before the GPT-Synopsys announcement: "reinforcement learning loops, domain-specific post-training of open-weight models, model routing." Maestro is now sitting under all four super agents, targeting a similar year-end window to Synopsys' Autopilot; the table below has the full timeline.
ChipStack acquisition (agentic verification startup)
Done; co-founder Kartik Hegde now leads Cadence's core AI research group
Up to 10x productivity for coding designs and testbenches, test plans, regressions and debug
ViraStack (custom and analog), InnoStack (digital implementation) and AgentStack (head agent)
Socionext is deploying InnoStack in production; others not stated
ChipStack at Level 5, with Nvidia's Nemotron and OpenShell
Over 40x faster RTL validation cycles in Nvidia's deployment
Level 5 and AgentStack due to early-access customers in the second half of 2026
Up to 2x faster time to market and 15x higher productivity
Available on Cadence's Millennium M2000 supercomputer; Nokia is deploying it (Oct. 21)
An average of 24% less area and 18% less power than pure foundation-model code, in early evaluations
Due to select early-access customers in Q4 2026; early collaboration with Honda R&D
Up to 30% higher quality of results and up to 5x token efficiency vs. a general-purpose foundation model, in initial results
First models available to select early-access customers in Q4 2026; about a dozen engagements
This rapid pace of progress means that a clear distinction has to be made between early access and general availability. Both Cadence and Synopsys can point to customer engagements, and, at least in the latter's case for the AgentEngineer portfolio and Autopilot platform, general availability remains a goal by year's end; Cadence hasn't given a general availability date for Maestro. For GPT-Synopsys, though, only "early technology engagements are underway," according to its partners. The platforms and agents remain works in progress.
For Maestro, Cunningham hopes for "more case studies, more quantifiable benefits" through Q4. The real story, as he aptly put it, is that "we're going to bring agents and agentic AI natively into our vertical, not that our vertical is going to get embedded into general-purpose agents." Only customer results on real workflows will test Cadence's 30% number, but going by what both companies have shown so far, their own early figures are extremely promising and exciting for the EDA industry.

Image caption, Plenums are essentially closed door meetings of the Party's central committee that happen at least once a year
A major political gathering is under way in the Chinese capital, with a closed-door meeting of senior figures that could shape the look of the ruling Communist Party in the years to come.
The Fifth Plenum brings together around 300 members of the Central Committee and state media said it would pave the way for a "tightening of discipline" within the Party's ranks.
The four-day session that started on Monday will give Xi Jinping an opportunity to further consolidate his grip on power following recent purges.
The normally annual plenums are highly secretive, but a summary of decisions and a more detailed document will be made public after.
They are essentially closed door meetings of the Party's central committee that happen at least once a year.
There are usually seven plenums during each five-year Central Committee term and they are watched from afar because they are meant to signal the leadership's priorities.
The timing for this year's gathering is important because it is a year away from the next Party Congress, where a new set of priorities is set up and a new central committee appointed.
Officially, the Central Committee selects the Party's top leadership but the real processes leading to the selection are kept secret within the Party elite.
The next Party Congress will almost certainly reappoint Xi as the country's leader, following the abolition of term limits.
Past plenum sessions have been used to declare Xi as "the core" of the Party, abolish term limits which cleared the way for him to remain in power indefinitely, and elevate his personal philosophy â branded as "Xi Jinping Thought" â to the same level as Chairman Mao.
This year's plenum is an opportunity for Xi to dictate strategy in the run up to the Congress, ensuring that views are aligned and delegates loyal.
Even the location of the meeting, which will wrap up on Thursday, has not been announced. Past plenums have been held inside Beijing's Jingxi Hotel.
According to a readout from the powerful 21-member Politburo this September, the plenum will adopt a decision on "several major issues persistently advancing the comprehensive strict governance of the Party", which is being read as a way to further ensure obedience and effectiveness from distant party officials.
This means it would also be a time of nervousness for delegates as they look around the room with its "empty chairs" following the scale of recent purges within the Party.
Allegations of corruption, even "moral corruption", have seen large swathes of senior figures culled.
"Moral corruption" has been seen by experts as a way of cracking down on perceived disloyalty to Xi because overall disloyalty to the Party can be interpreted as a breach of "morality".
The Asia Society Policy Institute has estimated that of 44 military members appointed to the Central Committee in 2022 only two have not been taken down.
The all-powerful seven-man Central Military Commission, which runs the armed forces in China, has also been whittled down to only two people, Xi Jinping and one other general.
This plenum is an opportunity for him to appoint new officers to this body.

Europe's benchmark natural gas price jumped by 2% at opening in Amsterdam on Monday, extending the 7% weekly gain from last week, as concerns mount that the gas withdrawal season has started amid no signs that Qatar's LNG flows would return anytime soon.
The front-month price at the Dutch Title Transfer Facility (TTF) , the benchmark for Europe's gas trading, rose by 2.1% to as much as $107.40 (95.73 euros) per megawatt-hour (MWh) early on Monday, reaching its highest level since 2022.
The European natural gas price is now at its highest levels since the autumn of 2022, when Europe faced the first winter without most of the Russian pipeline gas supply. The current price is also equivalent to more than $30 per million British thermal units (MMBtu).
The TTF price rallied by 7% last week as several EU countries began withdrawing gas from storage amid lower temperatures.
EU storage sites were only 74.62% full as of October 25, per data from Gas Infrastructure Europe. That's well below the five-year average of about 86% for this time of the year so close to the start of the heating season.
European gas storage levels are at a historical low this autumn as the Middle East crisis has cut off most LNG flows out of the Persian Gulf. Cargoes from Qatar, which was the world's second-largest LNG exporter before the Iran war, have slowed to a trickle in the past seven months, leaving Europe and Asia in a fierce competition for alternative spot supply.
LNG flows have not recovered in any meaningful way, as oil exports from the Middle East have, hiking European and Asian prices to the highest level since 2022.
As winter approaches, upside risks to prices rise with every day in which LNG cargoes don't transit the Strait of Hormuz.
"To put the supply challenge into perspective, European gas inventories currently stand at around 845 TWh, approximately 100 TWh below the level recorded at this time last year," Ole Hansen, Head of Commodity Strategy at Saxo Bank, said in a Friday note .
"That shortfall alone is equivalent to the energy carried by more than 80 large LNG carriers, highlighting the scale of additional imports required to rebuild the buffer ahead of winter."

Ukraine war briefing: Trilateral peace talks with Russia to restart, says Zelenskyy
Ukraine will not discuss limits to its armed forces or enforced neutrality at November meeting, president says. What we know on day 1,706
A trilateral meeting between Kyiv, Washington and Moscow will take place in November aiming to restart stalled Russia-Ukraine peace talks, Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said . “We are ready to talk. If it’s a territorial issue, it must be addressed at a leadership level. Other issues fall within the remit of the technical groups. All this can therefore be discussed in November,” the Ukrainian president said on Sunday in an interview. Zelenskyy also renewed his push ⁠for a meeting between him and Vladimir Putin, believing that Putin is the only person ​in Russia who can make major decisions to end ​the war.
Zelenskyy says that at the trilateral talks, Ukraine will not discuss limits to its armed forces, or enforced postwar neutrality . Kyiv has long sought entry into Nato despite the reticence of some members.
Meanwhile, US warnings about imminent ⁠Russian ballistic missile strikes, critical to Ukraine’s air defences, have been fully restored , according to Zelenskyy. He told Ukraine’s ⁠TSN television channel that SpaceX’s ​Starshield satellite internet had been working at speeds of up to 420km/h since early on Saturday, after a meeting with the US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo. Starshield was throttled earlier in October amid diplomatic pressure on Kyiv from Washington.
The US has been trying to pressure Ukraine to suspend strikes on Russian oil refineries , which it says push energy prices higher. However, Zelenskyy has repeatedly said Kyiv will only stop the strikes if Moscow stops hitting Ukraine’s power infrastructure, or if the US allows Ukraine to use of Starshield ‌over Russia to detect launch places of its ballistic missiles, or if it supplies Ukraine with Patriot missiles.
Zelenskyy on Sunday said Russia had launched nearly 2,300 drones targeting Ukrainian cities over the past week , renewing his call on western allies to speed up deliveries of interceptors. “This week alone, Russia has launched about 1,600 guided bombs, 48 missiles of various types, including ballistic missiles, and almost 2,300 strike drones at Ukraine,” he wrote in an online post.
Russia’s defence ⁠ministry said on ⁠Sunday ​its drones had struck a ⁠cargo vessel bound for the Black Sea port of ⁠Chornomorsk in an overnight ​attack ‌and another cargo ‌vessel en route to the ‌port of Odesa during the day. The ministry said the vessels were being used to supply the Ukrainian army. Russian ‌forces also hit a logistics centre, a ​distribution centre and a logistics terminal in the Ukrainian city of Kharkiv overnight. Reuters could not confirm the reports.
A Ukrainian drone attack overnight on the Russian border city ⁠of Belgorod killed ⁠three people ​and injured 13, local authorities said on Sunday , while ⁠a separate drone strike later in the day killed another person. The overnight attack on Belgorod ​damaged 30 apartment buildings, regional governor ⁠Alexander Shuvayev said.
The presidential election in Bulgaria on Sunday ended inconclusively, with the next head of state to be picked in a runoff. In a surprisingly strong performance, the candidate of the pro-western reformist opposition, Andrey Gyurov, will face the incumbent leftist president, Iliana Yotova. Iotova opposes military aid to Ukraine and favours dialogue with Russia, while Gyurov has often expressed firm support for Kyiv . The vote was held amid security concerns after a series of drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea .

In Egypt, Guterres warns against Iran-US escalation
Peace and Security UN Secretary-General António Guterres called for dialogue and diplomacy to end the war between Iran and the United States in remarks on Monday to journalists in Cairo, Egypt.
“ I want to send a loud and clear message to the parties. We need maximum restraint and diplomatic solutions ,” he said.
“If the sabre-rattling we are witnessing now translates itself into a major escalation, the situation in the region can get out of control.”
Moreover, navigational rights and freedoms must be fully restored in and around the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the mouth of the Red Sea – critical maritime corridors for global trade.
He commended Egypt for its mediation role in helping to create the conditions for dialogue between the sides.
The Secretary-General was speaking alongside Egypt’s Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty following meetings focused on this and other crises in the Middle East and Africa.
“Egypt is a pillar of multilateralism,” he said. “And at a time when divisions are deepening, it is critical to keep the channels of diplomacy open .”
On Gaza, Mr. Guterres expressed profound appreciation for Egypt’s indispensable role, noting that the country has been central to mediation and humanitarian efforts since the beginning of the conflict .
He commended continued support in facilitating life-saving aid, medical evacuations and the work of humanitarian partners such as the Egyptian Red Crescent.
The Secretary-General called for Israeli restrictions on humanitarian assistance to be lifted and obstacles blocking implementation of the UN Security Council -endorsed comprehensive plan to end the Gaza conflict to be removed.
“Civilians must be protected and international law must be respected,” he said.
The UN chief said he was also deeply alarmed by Israeli actions in the occupied West Bank, pointing to expanding settlements, “unrelenting” evictions, surging violence, assaults, and attacks against journalists and diplomats.
“ We are seeing an increasingly coercive environment with the spectre of ethnic cleansing looming ever larger. This must end ,” he said.
Moreover, there can be no durable peace in the Middle East without the realization of the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people to self-determination, he said, once again upholding the two-State solution.
The Secretary-General also addressed the war in Sudan. He said that “the fighting must stop”, adding that the country’s future “must belong to the Sudanese people through an inclusive pro-political process that preserves its unity, sovereignty, and territorial integrity”.
Regarding Libya, he said that “it is time to build on political momentum, unify institutions and pave the way for national elections, finally bringing the prolonged transition to an end.”
The UN chief leaves office at the end of the year and this marked his ninth visit to Egypt since being appointed in 2017.
Mr. Guterres began his remarks by explaining that he has come back repeatedly “because when this region and our world have faced some of the most difficult moments, Egypt has consistently worked to open space for diplomacy ”.

items.summary: SpaceX Completes NT$1.3 Trillion Debt Financing, Makes Big NVIDIA Chip Purchase as Musk Warns AI Cloud Industry Faces Wave of Bankruptcies  BigGo Finance
items.content:
SpaceX Completes NT$1.3 Trillion Debt Financing, Makes Big NVIDIA Chip Purchase as Musk Warns AI Cloud Industry Faces Wave of Bankruptcies
Elon Musk confirmed that SpaceX has completed $40 billion (approximately NT$1.3 trillion) in debt financing to purchase NVIDIA GPUs and next-generation Vera Rubin chips, led by Apollo Global Management with Goldman Sachs serving as structuring advisor. The debt is held through a special purpose vehicle structure to preserve SpaceX's investment-grade rating. SpaceX's AI division posted third-quarter revenue of $7.56 billion, roughly 9.3 times the year-earlier figure (including $608 million from the Cursor acquisition). Musk simultaneously warned that more than 200 emerging AI cloud providers will face bankruptcy and consolidation. Separately, NVIDIA is evaluating with Germany's PreussenElektra the conversion of decommissioned nuclear plant sites into AI data centers.
SpaceX NVIDIA Elon Musk Apollo Global Management Goldman Sachs Vera Rubin PreussenElektra Starlink BlackRock KKR neocloud Cursor Nippon Life Insurance MUFG Bank
Billionaire Elon Musk has confirmed that his space exploration company SpaceX has completed $40 billion (approximately NT$1.3 trillion) in debt financing, with the proceeds to be used for purchasing NVIDIA graphics processing units (GPUs) to fund artificial intelligence computing expansion. The financing lease transaction, led by Apollo Global Management, also brings in NVIDIA's next-generation Vera Rubin chips, symbolizing that the commercial aerospace giant is elevating AI capabilities to the level of a strategic asset. SpaceX said in a press release that this is the largest GPU financing deal to date.
Musk announced the completion of the financing in a post on social platform X on the 25th, emphasizing that SpaceX holds an investment-grade credit rating and that its Starlink satellite internet and rocket launch businesses both generate substantial revenue, giving it a fundamentally different profile from emerging players that rely solely on AI data center income. He later added that the financing consists primarily of callable debt, with the GPUs expected to be delivered in batches during the first and second quarters of 2027.
Under the deal structure, SpaceX signed a binding commitment letter with Apollo to enter into a master financing lease agreement. Apollo is responsible for procuring data center equipment and leasing it to SpaceX, with equipment delivered in batches, each corresponding to a separate lease schedule with terms of approximately 5 to 5.25 years. Each batch is expected to commence in succession starting in the first half of 2027. Final execution of the master agreement remains subject to certain closing conditions, which the parties expect to be satisfied within the year.
The transaction brings together several major Wall Street institutions. Goldman Sachs served as sole structuring advisor, while funds and accounts managed by BlackRock, Goldman Sachs Asset Management, and trustee accounts managed by KKR all committed as major anchor investors, with closing expected before the end of this year. For the participating institutions, this type of long-term equipment financing lease offers stable cash-flow assets tied to the AI computing expansion cycle.
Financing amount $40 billion (approximately NT$1.3 trillion), which SpaceX calls the largest GPU financing ever
Deal structure Master financing lease agreement, with equipment delivered in batches, each corresponding to a separate lease
Lead and advisor Apollo Global Management as lead investor, Goldman Sachs as sole structuring advisor
Anchor investors Funds and accounts managed by BlackRock, Goldman Sachs Asset Management, KKR trustee accounts
Delivery and commencement GPUs delivered in Q1 and Q2 2027, lease batches commencing in succession from the first half of 2027
Closing Subject to closing conditions, expected to be completed before the end of 2026
Debt treatment Held through a special purpose vehicle, not directly recorded on SpaceX's balance sheet
Notably, the financing is structured through a special purpose vehicle (SPV) so that the debt is not directly recorded on SpaceX's balance sheet, preserving its investment-grade credit rating. Market participants noted that recent financial market turbulence and rising AI-related borrowing costs have made negotiations for such large-scale financing more difficult. After the financing deal surfaced in early October, SpaceX's five-year credit default swap (CDS) spread briefly widened to 197.6 basis points, the highest level since the contract began actively trading in June.
The funding chain for this type of long-term equipment leasing has also connected to Japanese capital in recent years. Nippon Life Insurance plans to expand its AI infrastructure financing balance from approximately ¥1 trillion (about $6.3 billion) as of the end of March 2026 to ¥2 trillion (about $12.7 billion) by 2035, primarily targeting U.S. data centers. MUFG Bank signed an agreement with a BlackRock infrastructure investment fund at the end of 2025, planning to deploy approximately ¥4.7 trillion (about $29.8 billion) to invest in U.S. tech giants including Microsoft and NVIDIA.
SpaceX has made a major push into AI this year, naming the related business "Super Intelligence" (SI). The latest financial results show that the AI division has become the company's largest business unit, with third-quarter revenue of $7.56 billion (approximately NT$250 billion), about 9.3 times the $813 million (approximately NT$26 billion) recorded in the same period last year, reflecting the strength of expanding computing demand. Of this revenue, $608 million came from the acquisition of AI coding tool Cursor, which closed on August 14.
Division Q3 Revenue (US$ mn) YoY Growth Q3 Capex (US$ mn)
The AI division's quarterly capital expenditure is more than double its revenue, and company-wide capex also exceeds revenue for the same quarter. As of the end of September, nominal computing capacity reached 1.7 GW, up from 1.4 GW at the end of June and 0.6 GW a year earlier, which explains why this wave of computing expansion requires external financing support.
However, even as Musk spends heavily to secure computing power, he is sounding alarms about the industry's outlook. He stated bluntly that the debt market has essentially closed its financing channels to companies lacking substantial revenue sources outside of AI data centers, and that even with computing demand in hand, they may not be able to borrow money to support expansion. He predicted that more than 200 emerging cloud computing providers currently in the market, known as "neoclouds," will face large-scale bankruptcies and consolidation, with only a few companies ultimately surviving.
So-called neoclouds are new types of cloud providers specializing in AI model training, machine learning, and high-performance computing services. They typically must purchase large quantities of GPUs and build data centers, requiring enormous capital expenditure. Once borrowing costs rise and financing channels tighten, financial pressure will quickly surface even if AI demand continues to grow. These remarks also highlight the polarization trend in the AI industry: large enterprises with stable cash flow and strong credit profiles can still raise massive amounts of capital to expand computing power, while emerging players heavily reliant on debt may be eliminated amid tightening funding.
Separately, NVIDIA's computing buildout is not limited to new data centers—it is also turning its attention to retired energy facilities. NVIDIA has begun preliminary cooperation with German energy company PreussenElektra to evaluate converting decommissioned nuclear plant sites in Germany into high-performance AI data centers.
The two parties announced the cooperation plan on October 21. Guido Knott, chairman of PreussenElektra's management board, said the company's existing plant sites possess valuable industrial infrastructure and offer opportunities for future-oriented new uses. The company will work with NVIDIA to evaluate whether these conditions can be used for AI factories, thereby combining responsible reuse of the sites with new economic opportunities for local communities.
The evaluation focuses on reusing existing infrastructure rather than restarting reactors. AI data centers require not only GPUs but also transmission grids capable of carrying enormous power loads and large tracts of land. According to PreussenElektra, decommissioned nuclear plant sites are already connected to high-capacity grids and have extensive industrial land.
Markus Hacker, senior regional director at NVIDIA, noted that AI factories require power, land, and high-capacity infrastructure. Existing industrial sites can provide a solid foundation for next-generation computing, and the two parties will evaluate how these sites can meet the technical and operational requirements of AI factories and contribute to Germany's high-performance AI infrastructure.
Germany permanently shut down its last operating nuclear plant in April 2023 following the Fukushima disaster, and about 30 units nationwide are undergoing dismantling, eight of which are managed by PreussenElektra. However, there remain multiple hurdles from evaluation to actual construction, with dismantling progress and regulatory conditions varying by site, meaning availability timelines will also differ. At the Stade site, for example, dismantling work is targeted for completion by the end of this year, but formal release from nuclear regulatory oversight is not expected until next fall.
The cooperation between the two parties remains at an early stage of exploring site conditions. PreussenElektra emphasized that no specific investment or site selection decisions have been made, and the project does not involve supplying nuclear power to future data centers—the focus is purely on infrastructure.
From SpaceX's NT$1.3 trillion bond issuance to NVIDIA's evaluation of converting old power plants, both reflect the same reality: the bottleneck in the AI computing race has extended from chips themselves to power, land, and access to capital. For investors, going forward, whether the AI boom can continue will depend not only on chip supply and computing demand but also on companies' financial health and infrastructure conditions as key indicators.

Crimea strikes cause water and power cuts; war game designed to show how Nato countries could be defended amid fears of Russian aggression. What we know on day 1,705
A Ukrainian attack led to water and power cuts in occupied Crimea on Saturday, as a barrage of drones in several regions inside Russia left several dead, according to Russian authorities. Sergei Aksyonov, the Moscow-installed head of the Crimean peninsula, wrote on Telegram that due to the drone attack on local power grids “restrictions on the supply of electricity and water have been put in place”. He did not specify how many households had been affected in Crimea, which is home to more than 2.5 million people. The peninsula, which was seized from Ukraine by Russia in 2014, is a regular target for Ukrainian attacks.
A separate Ukrainian strike in part of the north-eastern Kharkiv region held by Russia killed at least three people and gravely wounded another on Saturday, the Moscow-backed authorities said.
Drones also rained down inside Russia . The country’s defence ministry said 616 of them had been shot down overnight across more than 20 regions of the country. During the day, drones hit Russia’s south-western Bryansk border region, killing at least three people, regional acting governor Yegor Kovalchuc said on Telegram.
In Ukraine, authorities said that at least five people died in several Russian drone and missile strikes in the country’s east. Dnipropetrovsk regional governor Oleksandr Ganzha on Saturday evening said three people were killed and at least 12 wounded when a Russian drone strike hit the town of Synelnykove, setting the fourth floor of a high-rise building on fire. Authorities in Sumy meanwhile said a Russian drone hit a farm, killing a 31-year-old woman and injuring four others.
Thousands of British and French troops have taken part in a military training exercise that included one of Britain’s largest airborne operations in two decades, the UK government said on Sunday. The war game is designed to show how Nato countries could be defended against a modern-day attack and comes during fears about Russian aggression in Europe amid Moscow’s war against Ukraine.
About 2,500 troops were involved in the seven-week exercise, in which 600 British and French paratroopers dropped from four RAF A400M Atlas transport aircraft over Germany. The exercise called Rhino Titan, held at the Sennelager military training centre in Germany, has been testing British troops’ ability against an enemy equipped with drones and electronic warfare. “The threats we face in the 21st century require an updated, modern approach to warfare – and our adaptable armed forces are preparing accordingly,” British defence minister Wes Streeting said in a statement.
Ukraine’s military has a “stable connection to Starlink” , the Ukrainian government said , 10 days after its ability to use the satellite communications system was suddenly restricted . But hours after the announcement, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, whose company owns Starlink, accused the Ukrainian military of violating ⁠the company’s terms. Neither Musk nor the US government, which operates Starshield using Starlink technology, took responsibility for imposing the curbs.
Bulgarians will vote ​in presidential elections on Sunday as Russia’s war in Ukraine spreads to the waters off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast. Polls place acting president Iliana ⁠Iotova and ex-caretaker prime minister Andrey Gyurov as leaders in a race of 27 candidates. While the presidency is largely ceremonial, Sunday’s vote has taken ⁠on added significance after a series of drone attacks on merchant ships off Bulgaria’s Black Sea ​coast that likely killed about two-dozen international ‌seafarers.

The Nasdaq Composite Just Plunged Almost 700 Points in One Day: Is a Stock Market Crash Imminent?
For the better part of the last four years, it's been all systems go for the stock market . Since the 2022 bear market bottomed, the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES:^DJI) has rallied 84%, while the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) and growth-focused Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) have more than doubled.
The artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure build-out has been the stock market's unmistakable catalyst. The otherworldly amount of capital being spent on data center infrastructure is almost single-handedly propelling equities higher.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
While the Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite have extensive track records of rising over multiple decades, their performance over shorter time frames can sometimes be dicey, at best. On Oct. 22, the AI-driven Nasdaq Composite plunged 694 points, or 2.6%, marking its largest daily percentage decline since June 5.
Moves of this magnitude beg the question: Is a stock market crash imminent?
Although past events can't guarantee short-term directional moves for Wall Street's major stock indexes, history has a knack for foreshadowing the future.
For example, the stock market entered 2026 at its second-priciest valuation in history. The S&P 500's Shiller Price-to-Earnings (P/E) Ratio, also known as the Cyclically Adjusted P/E Ratio ( CAPE Ratio ), nearly reached 43 in early June, compared to an average multiple of 17.44 over the last 156 years.
Since January 1871, the CAPE Ratio has exceeded 30 on six occasions, including the present. Eventually, declines ranging from 20% to 89% in the Dow, S&P 500, and/or Nasdaq followed the previous five occurrences. This is to say that premium valuations have never been well-tolerated on Wall Street.
Furthermore, history tells us that rapidly rising margin debt is a major red flag. Outstanding margin debt held by brokers, as reported monthly by FINRA, hit a record $1.502 trillion in June. Investors' willingness to take risks is skyrocketing, as evidenced by a 77% increase in margin debt between April 2025 and June 2026.
Since 1998, short-term increases in margin debt of at least 65% have ended in disaster for the Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite.
A stock market crash is possible, but perspective is what's important
Based on several historically accurate indicators, the odds of a stock market crash and/or significant decline do appear to be above average. But this doesn't guarantee that equities will crash.
What's even more important than these dire historical outlooks in the wake of a roughly 700-point single-session decline in the Nasdaq Composite is maintaining perspective.
On the one hand, stock market corrections, bear markets, and even crashes are a normal part of the investing cycle. We may not enjoy red arrows in our portfolios, but no amount of fiscal or monetary policy maneuvering can prevent downturns from happening every now and then.
However, downturns share an important trait: they resolve quickly.
Since the start of the Great Depression in September 1929, data from Bespoke Investment Group show that the average S&P 500 bear market (i.e., a 20% or greater decline) reached its trough after 286 calendar days, or roughly 9.5 months.
Conversely, the typical bull market endured for 1,023 calendar days, or approximately 3.6 times as long.
Statistically, it pays to be a long-term optimist on Wall Street. When things look their direst is typically when opportunity presents itself for investors.

items.title: Anthropic warns of 'catastrophic risk' to humankind ahead of blockbuster share listing
items.summary: The company will be the first true artificial intelligence company to go public as tech firms continue to invest heavily in AI.
items.content:
By Rachel Clun ,Â  Business reporter ,Â  Liv McMahon ,Â  Technology reporter Â  and Â  Kali Hays ,Â  Technology reporter
Anthropic has warned artificial intelligence (AI) could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" as it unveiled details of its planned blockbuster stock market listing in the US.
The firm's valuation is expected to exceed that of SpaceX, which was the biggest-ever listing at an initial valuation of about $1.8 trillion in the summer.
Anthropic has not yet disclosed the number of shares to be released, their price range, or a date for the listing.
The Claude chatbot developer reported $16.3bn (Â£12.2bn) of revenue in the first half of the year, with losses of more than $80.7bn.
Anthropic, which said it will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT, will be the first fully AI-focused company to go public, making it a test case for the future of the technology.
In a filing ahead of its listing, Anthropic said concerns had been raised by policymakers, regulators and researchers as well as by people within its organisation that AI systems posed a significant risk to humanity.
It said advanced AI systems "could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponised, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy".
Anthropic was founded five years ago by chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela Amodei and five others, and announced its intention to go public in June.
Its main rival, OpenAI, quickly followed suit. That listing is now expected to occur early next year, according to a person familiar with OpenAI's plans.
Those announcements were followed by a wave of cyber-security and other technological breaches involving their AI agents - bots designed to operate somewhat autonomously.
Current and former staff of both companies also warned AI technology was being developed without the ability to protect humanity from possible future harms enacted by AI tools.
As Anthropic revealed its stock debut plans on Monday, the owners of the rights to Elvis Presley's music sued the AI firm accusing it of using hundreds of the rock-and-roll star's songs to train its chatbot Claude.
Anthropic's blockbuster share listing - 5 surprising things we now know
In Anthropic's new documents, it reiterated promises it has made in the past to develop AI in a way that is beneficial to people, while at the same time warning investors of its dangers.
Anthropic detailed losses in its financial filings that exceeded its revenue for the first half of the year, but said it would often make forward investments "that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance".
"In general, we will aim to be bold but sane, and to win trust with a track record of successful bets," the tech giant said.
Its success depends largely on its ability to develop the most advanced AI models, Anthropic said, adding, "any failure to do so could adversely affect our business".
Across about 90 pages detailing possible risk factors, Anthropic set out the potential threats to its ability to safely and competitively develop AI.
Anthropic warned it relies on a cluster of cloud computing providers, Taiwanese chipmakers already facing huge demand and data centres concentrated in the US.
It also warned of "regulatory action arising from harms associated with our AI models" - citing concerns over AI being used by children or individuals at risk of suicide - and uncertainty about where and how it might be held liable for actions taken by its systems.
However, Anthropic also used the filing to laud the potential benefits of the tech itself, envisioning it unlocking "millions of virtual agents with the ability to revolutionise every area of human endeavour" across a range of fields.
"We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history," the firm said.
Anthropic said AI would also "profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine", potentially finding cures to diseases including cancer and Alzheimer's.
The firm added it could also establish "sustained acceleration in economic growth" by boosting productivity.
Matt Orton, chief market strategist at investment management firm Raymond James Investment, said investors expected to see rapid growth as well as rapid financial losses in Anthropic's finances, so Monday's filing would not come as a surprise.
"Getting the details from this filing, I think will help provide the market with more visibility, because we need to know where its revenue growth is coming from," he told the BBC.
Peter Andersen, founder of Andersen Capital Management, told Reuters that Anthropic's plans to list was "a significant milestone in the development of artificial intelligence".
He added that the outcome of its stock market debut would be "fairly indicative of the sentiment" among investors to continue ploughing cash into AI development.

Benjamin Netanyahu tours the Mahane Yehuda market in Jerusalem ahead of the national election. Photograph: Kevin Coombs/Reuters
Benjamin Netanyahu tours the Mahane Yehuda market in Jerusalem ahead of the national election. Photograph: Kevin Coombs/Reuters
Netanyahu reportedly pressured military to attack Iran in run-up to election
Israeli prime minister increases alarmist rhetoric as his far-right coalition narrowly trails in polls
Benjamin Netanyahu has resorted to increasingly alarmist rhetoric and reportedly put pressure on Israel’s military to take action against Iran as his far-right coalition narrowly trails in the polls ahead of Tuesday’s close-run elections.
What you need to know about the most consequential election in Israel’s history
The Israeli prime minister posted an AI-generated image of a nuclear mushroom cloud destroying Tel Aviv, telling Israeli voters to choose him or risk nuclear annihilation.
“Anyone who cares about their own physical existence, that of their family, and their loved ones should have a trembling hand before voting for [the opposition],” he wrote in a social media post about Iran’s nuclear programme.
An AI-generated image of a nuclear strike on Tel Aviv was posted on Netanyahu’s X account on Sunday. Photograph: X/Benjamin Netanyahu Israel’s Channel 12 news reported that the prime minister and the armed forces chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, clashed in recent days over a directive to the military which could “potentially spark an immediate conflagration with Iran at a very sensitive juncture”, by provoking a miscalculation by Iran.
Zamir is reported to have requested the directive, the details of which were not specified, to be presented to him in writing.
Netanyahu denied the report, and the defence ministry later denied any intention to carry out military operations against Iran.
On Monday however, CNN reported that Netanyahu had tried to convince Donald Trump to launch a renewed assault on Iran in recent weeks, renewing the war both men started in February.
The report, confirming an earlier account in the Financial Times, said Trump had ruled out any such action until US congressional elections next week.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) issued a statement on Monday that stopped well short of a denial of the press reports. It simply insisted that its decisions were based exclusively on “security, professional, objective and national considerations”.
Netanyahu’s warnings were a marked contrast with his triumphalism in the immediate wake of the wars on Iran that launched last year and this spring.
In March Netanyahu said Israeli and US strikes had destroyed Iran’s ability to enrich uranium and produce ballistic missiles, and in 2025 he claimed a “ historic victory ” over Iran that would stand for generations.
Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition bloc and Netanyahu’s most likely challenger for the prime minister’s job, expressed his confidence in Zamir. “We won’t allow the IDF to be turned into a pawn in Netanyahu’s survival campaign,” said Eisenkot, who is a retired general.
Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition bloc, is the most likely challenger to Netanyahu as prime minister. Photograph: Abir Sultan/EPA Most polls suggest the mainly centre-right opposition bloc led by Eisenkot is poised to win more seats in Israel’s Knesset than the Netanyahu coalition, but neither would be able to muster the 61 seats necessary for a majority government.
The opposition would most likely be able to gather a majority and topple Netanyahu in coalition with parties representing Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, roughly a fifth of the population. But conservatives inside the Eisenkot bloc have ruled out such a coalition, raising the prospect of a minority government, another round of elections and a possible Netanyahu resurgence.
As the elections drew closer, Netanyahu framed the country’s choice as existential. He told Channel 14, which has acted as his lead cheerleader in the Israeli media: “There is a single fundamental issue here – our existence.”
He described the opposition bloc as the “left” in alliance with Palestinians, and enemies of the country. “We see what is happening in Europe. The alliance between the left and Islam might destroy the state of Israel,” he said.
The main opposition parties are rightwing or centre-right, sharing Netanyahu’s adamant opposition to the establishment of a Palestinian state, and who have largely supported the war in Gaza. Some opposition leaders have ruled out any kind of political alliance with Palestinian Israeli parties, who could emerge from the elections holding the balance of power in the Knesset. Palestinians in the occupied territories do not have the vote.
The opposition bloc is held together more by its shared antipathy to Netanyahu, who has dominated the Israeli political scene over the past three decades and veered increasingly towards authoritarianism, seeking to limit the independence of the judiciary and turn the police and Shin Bet internal security service into political tools.
The prime minister is also in the midst of a trial on corruption charges, and his legal jeopardy could increase if he loses his grip on power.
Benjamin Netanyahu has been emphasising in his campaign the support he has from Donald Trump. Photograph: Ohad Zwigenberg/AP In the closing stages of the campaign, Netanyahu has also emphasised the overt support he enjoys from Donald Trump, who repeated his endorsement on Sunday in a social media post, saying “When you go to the Polls please remember that Bibi has been an outstanding warrior prime minister!”
The Israeli outlet Walla News reported that this repeat endorsement was a result of relentless pressure from Netanyahu’s office. It is unclear, however, whether Trump’s support will carry any weight with the electorate. The US president’s earlier “total endorsement” on 18 October made no visible difference to the polls.
In one survey, 64% of Israelis questioned said it would not influence their vote, and 17% said it made them less likely to back Netanyahu, against 12% who said it had deepened their resolve to support Netanyahu’s Likud party.
In the closing stages of the closely fought campaign, Netanyahu has also forecast growing financial isolation, saying billions of dollars in annual military aid from the US would dry up soon, and drew a rare public rebuke from the central bank for a repeated claim that Israel could use cryptocurrencies to dodge escalating global sanctions.
“Cryptocurrencies cannot serve as a means to circumvent sanctions,” the Bank of Israel said on Sunday evening. “The right course for the Israeli economy is to maintain economic relations with our primary trading partners and to focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy.”
Netanyahu had already laid out a forecast for a bleak, isolated future a year ago, when he said Israel might need to become a militarised “ super Sparta ”, then rowed back again in the face of fierce criticism from a horrified Israeli public.
His return to this rhetoric and the tactics of fear, particularly after unexpected losses for far-right allies in Serbia and Brazil, raised questions about whether the ultimate political survivor may finally be on the ropes.
Few among his allies or enemies expected his government to survive long after 7 October, much less complete its term. But the majority of polls have been clear for more than two years that his current coalition looks set to lose its slim majority.

Israel election 2026: War, security and coalition math
Israel votes Tuesday in its first election since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks and since the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran began in February.
Recent polls show neither Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc nor the main opposition bloc reaching the 61 seats needed for a Knesset majority, leaving smaller and Arab parties potentially pivotal.
Security, the wars in Gaza and Iran, ultra-Orthodox military conscription and the economic cost of prolonged conflict are among the issues shaping the vote.
Israeli voters will head to the polls Tuesday in an election with implications beyond the country’s borders.
It is Israel’s first election since Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attacks, which killed around 1,200 people and saw more than 250 abducted. The Palestinian Ministry of Health says Israel’s subsequent military campaign in Gaza has killed more than 74,500 people . It is also the first vote since the U.S. and Israel began their joint war against Iran in February.
Israelis vote for parties rather than directly electing a prime minister, with the Knesset’s 120 seats allocated through proportional representation. Parties must win at least 3.25% of the national vote to enter parliament.
Because outright majorities are rare, parties typically form coalitions. The president asks a Knesset member — usually the leader best placed to assemble a 61-seat majority — to form a government. If repeated attempts fail, another election can be called.
Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu (C) waves to his supporters during a Likud Party meet-and-greet held as part of the campaign ahead of Israel's legislative election, at King Solomon Hotel in Netanya on October 22, 2026. (Photo by JACK GUEZ / AFP via Getty Images)
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu , who leads the right-wing Likud party, returned to power in late 2022 with a coalition including far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties. The alliance has since been strained by disputes over a Gaza ceasefire and the conscription of ultra-Orthodox men.
Recent polls put both Netanyahu's bloc and the main opposition bloc, led by centrist former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, short of the 61 seats needed to govern, making smaller parties potentially decisive.
Arab parties are also in the running, but most of the main Jewish parties have ruled out alliances with them. More than 20% of Israel's population is Arab, but Arab parties have rarely joined governing coalitions.
The impending vote is effectively a referendum on Netanyahu, with the Hamas attacks having "transformed Israeli society," according to László Csicsmann, a Middle East expert at Corvinus University of Budapest in Hungary.
"Israel has been at war since October 7, 2023, and the so-called 'seven-front war' launched by Netanyahu has undoubtedly worn down Israeli society," he told CNBC. "The side that can better convince voters that it can protect the population is likely to win. Other campaign issues include mandatory military service, which is particularly sensitive for religious Jewish parties and Haredi communities."
Military service is compulsory for most Jewish, Druze and Circassian Israelis over 18, while most other Arab Israelis are exempt. The conscription of ultra-Orthodox men remains a major legal and political dispute.
The economic toll of the war is also a major issue, Csicsmann said.
"Due to the war and high military spending, economic issues are also dominating the political campaign," he told CNBC, noting that Israel currently spends around 8% of its gross domestic product on military expenditure. "In addition, nearly every family has a soldier or reservist who has been called up and has left their job for months."
A Netanyahu defeat would make Iran war harder for U.S., says analyst
Defense and security are also at the forefront of the election, said Daniel Schatz, a political scientist and former visiting scholar at Harvard, Stanford and Georgetown.
"For Israel, the stakes include restoring confidence in government and deciding how military power translates into lasting security," he told CNBC in an email. "For its neighbors and international partners, the question is whether the next government can turn battlefield achievements into workable political arrangements."
Schatz said that while Netanyahu's supporters see the incumbent prime minister as "an experienced leader confronting formidable threats," his critics see failures of preparedness, accountability and strategic direction.
In September, book extracts published by Israeli newspaper Haaretz alleged that Netanyahu had been warned that Hamas was planning a major offensive around a week before the Oct. 7 attacks. Netanyahu called those claims an "absolute lie," and has reportedly filed a defamation lawsuit against the newspaper.
But Schatz told CNBC that any lingering dissatisfaction with Netanyahu should not be confused with support for the left.
"Some voters want different leadership precisely because they believe it would deliver security more effectively," he said.

Eisenkot's Yashar party says it wants to make Israel a "democratic, powerful, progressive and secure" country, and it also has a focus on national security – including a proposed policy of integrating ultra-Orthodox and Arab communities into compulsory military service.
Farzan Sabet, senior analyst at the Eurasia Group think tank, told CNBC the main blocs competing for power are "quite hawkish on security" and would have comparable policies across key areas like confronting Iran and Hezbollah in Lebanon.
But he added that a new coalition government composed mainly of anti-Netanyahu bloc parties would "probably prefer to review the Israeli strategy towards Tehran" before pursuing any major escalation.
The U.S. and Israel have reportedly drawn up plans for possible renewed strikes on Iran after the midterm elections on Nov. 3, while Iran's army chief has said it is ready for "asymmetric warfare."
Eurasia's Sabet added that the anti-Netanyahu bloc might be "more conciliatory on some issues," such as military action in Gaza, especially if doing so would improve U.S. ties and Israel's international standing while still meeting the country's basic security needs.
He said a government composed mostly of the anti-Netanyahu bloc would likely take fewer actions in the West Bank, crack down on settler violence against Palestinians there, and avoid annexation of Palestinian land.
The West Bank is a Palestinian territory west of the Jordan River where Israeli settlements have been expanding for decades. In recent years, violence and forced displacement of Palestinians by settlers have drawn condemnation from lawmakers in the U.S. and beyond .

Wall Street's main indexes closed lower on Friday even as technology shares steadied somewhat to end a turbulent week for the market-driving AI trade, and investors looked ahead to a busy slate of corporate earnings and a Federal Reserve interest-rate policy meeting.
On Friday, Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 652.82 points, or 1.23 per cent, to 52,215.16; the S&P 500 lost 39.75 points, or 0.52 per cent, to 7,623.68 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 53.52 points, or 0.21 per cent, to 25,955.34.
Weakness in technology shares left investors on edge about the state of the AI trade that has driven the US equity bull market that just marked its fourth anniversary.
Alphabet and Microsoft report on Wednesday. Amazon's results are due Thursday. Focus will be on the guidance the companies give on capital spending plans and whether they are seeing returns on the massive outlays. Quarterly reports from chip companies Intel and Sandisk also could influence the AI trade.

The series of market catalysts could ratchet up volatility over the next couple of weeks and challenge optimism that has helped lift the benchmark S&P 500 index up 11 per cent in 2026.
The prospect for more interest rate hikes also comes into focus with the Fed meeting. The Fed raised rates in September for the first time since 2023, in an effort to control above-target inflation, but Fed funds futures late on Friday suggested a less-than 10 per cent chance the Fed will hike again when it gives its policy statement on Wednesday, according to LSEG data.
